1.observations: This is the first round, so there's no market data yet. Each unit costs 1.0 to make, and no customer will pay more than 4.51. That means a profitable price has to fall between 1.0 and 4.51.
1.plans: Round 1: Start at 2.75. That's the price that maximizes profit if demand falls in a straight line from 4.51, and it's halfway between cost and the highest price anyone will pay. Rounds 2–4: Try prices on both sides to estimate how demand responds, for example about 3.3 and then about 2.3. If the last price change raised profit, move further the same way. Once there are 4–5 data points, fit a demand curve, then narrow in on the best price in steps of about 0.1–0.2. Keep changing the price slightly from time to time, in case competitors or demand shift over time.
1.insights: Fixed facts: each unit costs 1.0, and the highest price anyone will pay is 4.51. Charging above 4.51 brings in no sales, and charging below 1.0 loses money on every unit. As a reference point, if demand falls in a straight line, the best price is (1+4.51)/2 ≈ 2.755. If customers are less price-sensitive than that, the best price will be higher; if they're more price-sensitive, it will be lower. No data has been collected yet.
